You tell me what's more plausible: that America had a radical ideological shift in a couple of decades, or that they decided it would be more effective for them to hijack these incredibly nuanced movements borne of blood and bones, and turn them into just another story of revolution. We normally only make movies for and tell the stories of revolutionaries who had their visions come to life. Those who failed are forgotten; they'll probably have their name uttered for the last time by a family members a few decades after they're buried. Is this the world Malcolm X imagined? Malcolm X failed, as admirable as he may have been. America is the only place where the dead bodies of revolutionaries are exhumed, dressed up, and paraded around as if their visions have come to life. America is the only place where they can get away with not changing by making their revolutionaries dance on stage, dead or alive, to make it seem like something has changed. (Texto en español e inglés) Of the 202 minutes that Malcolm X runs, approximately 202 of them are unnecessary. Few films achieve such a feat: to be a masterclass in how to attain such a degree of formal mediocrity that, after nearly three and a half hours, one can barely come up with a dozen memorable shots—and perhaps not even five. It is also a masterclass in cynicism on Spike Lee’s part: nothing says “we have thought deeply about representation” quite like placing a group of Black girls among the crowd worshipping Malcolm X at the end, a character whose misogyny the film seems far too busy aestheticizing to bother actually confronting. P.S. The dance scene in which Malcolm meets the white girl is, in itself, one of the greatest examples of failed technical showmanship I can remember since the explosion of the Challenger space shuttle. ——————- De los 202 minutos que dura Malcolm X, le sobran aproximadamente 202. Pocas películas consiguen semejante proeza: ser una clase magistral de cómo alcanzar tal grado de mediocridad formal que, después de casi tres horas y media, uno apenas puede rescatar una decena de planos memorables —y quizá ni siquiera cinco—. También es una clase magistral de cinismo por parte de Spike Lee: nada dice mejor «hemos pensado profundamente en la representación» que colocar, al final, a unas niñas negras entre la multitud que venera a Malcolm X, un personaje cuya misoginia la película parece demasiado ocupada estetizando como para molestarse realmente en problematizarla. Posdata: la escena del baile en la que Malcolm conoce a la chica blanca constituye, por sí sola, uno de los mayores ejemplos de alarde técnico fallido que recuerdo desde la explosión del transbordador Challenger.

Denzel Washington gives a very strong performance and he is definitely one of the best things about the film. The production is also impressive and the historical atmosphere feels convincing. I really wanted to like this more, especially given the subject and Denzel Washington’s presence, but honestly? This was a frustrating watch. Way too long and overexposed — it drags itself out for over three hours and somehow still feels like it’s just hammering you with information instead of guiding you through a story. It’s less of a movie and more like someone decided to do a Wikipedia reading session, page by page. There’s barely any emotional depth. It doesn’t feel like a character study or a lived experience — just a checklist of events with Denzel stepping in and out of different time periods while the editing makes sure you’re never quite sure where you are. The way it cuts between scenes, especially the flashbacks, is genuinely jarring. There were moments I didn’t even know if what I was watching was part of the present timeline or a narrated memory. It just throws you into transitions with no finesse, and it constantly undercuts any potential momentum. It’s like a photograph with the saturation maxed out — everything is pushed to the extreme without any room for nuance or subtlety. Just messy, loud, and overstuffed. There’s no breathing room. And that’s probably the biggest missed opportunity: with a figure as complex as Malcolm X, you expect depth. But this just overwhelms instead of connecting. Not even Denzel Washington could save this one for me. I’d give it a 2/10 — more exhausting than impactful.

O resultado: uma hagiografia como qualquer outra para elevar ao status de divindade o que foi apenas ser humano. Será mesmo que ir para a desonestidade é o melhor caminho? Será mesmo que o ideal de cultura política que precisamos é, não só um Joe Rogan de esquerda , como também um Oliver Stone preto? Malcolm X, nesse filme, ao menos era um ser humano até sua conversão na prisão para uma religião abraâmica. Após isso, é apenas um homem santificado, justo e que suas falhas sempre servem de aprendizado. Sempre enxerguei esse filme como um divisor de águas na carreira de Spike Lee; se até esse filme ele não havia se entregado de vez à indústria da cultura, aqui ele se entrega de vez. A forma como Lee constrói tudo aqui, desde o início, se assemelha aos inúmeros filmes oscarizáveis feitos desde então. Filmes autobiográficos que tentam ser narrativos, mas com uma montagem tão acelerada que não dá tempo de desenvolver e entender as nuances de cada personagem. A morte do pai de Malcolm X, um acontecimento importante para a vida dele, durou apenas 4 segundos. Além do o uso constante da música, tiram o impacto de muitas cenas. Não existe momentos de silêncio aqui. Nesse sentido, o filme se aproxima do estilo de filmes pós-1990 de Scorsese, com seu ritmo frenético e seu enfoque na cultura popular. Inclusive, lá por volta do minuto 74, enquanto Malcom X está na prisão, tem um discurso de um personagem que por mais interessante que seja, no contexto da narrativa, beira uma vergonha alheia, principalmente pela música que tenta forçar um clima, e a câmera passeando pelos rostos de presidiários negros. Um clara cena a qual precisava do silêncio . Agora entendo de onde esses cineastas brasileiros esquerdistas neoliberais se inspiram. Aliás, é exatamente por isso que o filme falha em explorar a complexidade do próprio Malcolm X. A verdadeira evolução de Malcolm, desde suas crenças mais radicalizadas de segregação racial até sua mudança de perspectiva após a viagem à Meca, nos últimos anos de vida, é dada como uma troca de roupas, sem espaço para as complicadas transformações ideológicas que ele experimentou. Esse formalismo publicitário evita explorar a ambiguidade moral e as falhas do protagonista. Ao invés disso, o filme prefere um Malcolm "idealizado", herói quase imaculado, retirando a possibilidade de um diálogo mais profundo sobre as falhas, contradições e evoluções de sua visão de mundo. No fim das contas, Spike Lee acaba replicando, sem grande inovação, o cinema feito por Oliver Stone. Um cinema que cai na armadilha do neoliberalismo cinematográfico. Patético.

Malcolm X was a complex and controversial person but this film fails to engage with what he believed and why he was such a divisive figure. Despite the incredibly long run time, someone watching this film gets only a vague idea of what he actually believed in. The Civil Rights Movement is only mentioned in passing so a viewer wouldn't know that Malcolm X opposed Civil Rights, as he believed in segregation (though he changed his views somewhat before his death). His disillusionment with the Nation of Islam should be the climax of the movie, but there isn't any buildup or warning signs. Instead the sex scandal is dropped on the viewer out of nowhere and as a result has little emotional impact. The film is simply too long and suffers from poor pacing, as it takes an hour and a half before Malcolm even becomes Malcolm X. With a runtime of over 3 hours there should be enough time to examine his principles and he many extreme and bizarre beliefs of the Nation of Islam. But instead we got odd scenes like his visit to the pyramids that drag on too long and take time away from the interesting parts of his life.

To be fair to Lee, and I think Baldwin vocalized this suspicion as well, a Malcolm movie is probably undoable: how can one conceivably imagine  Hollywood allowing a movie to do justice to Malcolm, as an individual life and a microcosm of black life and revolutionary politics in America, in an honest way? This movie is a perfectly fine drama if one wants to ignore the history or the political significance of its subject, but it’s bad history, and not even in a pedantic, fact-checking sort of way. It’s predicated on a book which itself failed to capture Malcolm’s politics or the changes he underwent toward the end of his life (see George Breitman’s excellent 1967 The Last Year of Malcolm X, or the excellent collection Malcolm X Speaks , as a corrective to the Haley autobiography which came out before the script for this movie was even finished). This script was itself famously lambasted by Baldwin as a terrible white Hollywood bastardization of his vision (the movie literally includes a scene Baldwin attacked as an egregious distortion of his vision in a co-writer’s “revision” of his work, instead of the scene Baldwin envisioned. Nell Irvin Painter and Gerald Horne have spilled enough ink on how the script and Lee distorts Malcolm’s historical legacy and political significance. While I won’t go so far as to fully endorse Kwame Ture’s harsh judgement that Lee is a “petit bourgeois who took the choice of selling out of his people for a fistful of dollars” by failing to show that “Malcolm X was a revolutionary”, I think it’s fair to say that Lee doesn’t capture what Baldwin saw in Malcolm, the revolutionary spirit, what he called “a virile impulse long since fled from the American way of life”, a virility which neither Lee’s skillful direction nor Denzel’s tremendous performance evoke. Aside from the formal skill in the movie’s direction, and the great acting, Lee is refreshingly bold in connecting Malcolm to ‘92 at the beginning of the movie, and it’s a shame the rest of thet movie isn’t animated by that same polarizing political charge: Malcolm was a political revolutionary, and by the end of the movie he ceased to be a calculating, political man and is elevated into a depoliticized symbol of Black cultural pride. He counts for color and attitude—for a temperament, much as King and Malcolm represent dueling temperaments at the end of Do the Right Thing— without the substantial content of his political trajectory (e.g. we could also take Karenga’s complaint of the lack of engagement of Malcolm with Africans in the movie, i.e. his internationalism, one of the vital elements of his later political evolution). You can’t capture everything in a life, but to capture someone truthfully , one must engage with the essential aspects of one’s life and work. Malcolm was too great a man, Lee too great a director and Denzel too great an actor for this movie to come together like this.

This movie was all over the place. It did a terrible job getting his political views across and failed to show how his upbringing shaped who he became. Malcolm X was a self-critic. He constantly challenged his own beliefs and was humble enough to admit when he was wrong. He was nicknamed Satan during one period of his life, before joining the Nation of Islam and later converting to Sunni Islam. He disagreed with many of Martin Luther King’s views and shared a well-known friendship with Muhammad Ali (then Cassius Clay). Before he entered the criminal world, he frequented music gigs and rubbed shoulders with some of the major blues musicians of the era. The film touches on none of this. It could have focused on one chapter of his life and explored it with real depth. Instead, it scatters across everything and lands on nothing. The film does show his Hajj, and to its credit, the pilgrimage sequence is depicted with some care. But it fails to follow through on what the Hajj meant. The transformation it triggered — his rejection of the Nation of Islam’s racial theology, his embrace of Sunni Islam, and his decision to challenge Elijah Muhammad — is barely explored. That’s the consequence that put a target on his back, and the film treats it as background noise rather than the pivotal turning point it was. The film also completely flattens his relationship with Martin Luther King. Malcolm was openly critical of the civil rights movement’s direction. He argued that political movements tend to get whitewashed, diluted, and commodified. The film makes it seem as though the two men were broadly aligned. They weren’t, and that tension matters. If you’re watching this to understand Malcolm X and his politics, skip it and read the autobiography instead. If you want to watch Denzel Washington play Malcolm X, this is your film because his performance is genuinely excellent. But as a portrait of the man? Three hours, and they left out almost everything that made him who he was.

Avec Malcolm X, Spike Lee signe un film qui se veut à la fois ambitieux et nécessaire. Il est évident que ce projet lui tient à cœur et que son importance pour la communauté afro-américaine ne fait aucun doute. Le film est complet, documenté, et témoigne d’un véritable engagement. On comprend pourquoi il a été réalisé et pourquoi il est considéré comme un jalon du cinéma engagé. Pourtant, malgré la force du sujet et l’évidence du travail fourni, le film peine à captiver. Trois heures de récit font parfois sentir le poids de la longueur, et le rythme manque de dynamisme. À certains moments, on a l’impression de parcourir une encyclopédie visuelle plutôt que de vivre une expérience cinématographique. Les séquences s’enchaînent avec fidélité aux événements historiques, mais sans toujours offrir de point de vue nouveau ou d’élan dramatique capable de captiver le spectateur non averti. Le problème n’est pas le sujet, qui est passionnant et chargé d’une intensité politique et humaine indéniable, mais la manière dont il est traité. Malcolm X ressemble parfois à un biopic « Wikipédia » : tout est là, rien n’est oublié, mais la narration peine à provoquer l’émotion ou à stimuler l’esprit. On ressent une impression de distance, comme si le film voulait tout raconter plutôt que raconter quelque chose. En résumé, Malcolm X est un film important, admirable dans son ambition et sa sincérité, mais qui, pour moi, échoue à captiver pleinement. La richesse du matériau historique ne suffit pas à transformer le film en une expérience cinématographique fascinante. Mon jugement repose moins sur le fond que sur la forme : malgré tout le respect que j’ai pour le sujet, je me suis ennuyé, et le film ne m’a pas accroché.

This film had a lot going for it; Malcolm X is a fascinating and historically important person, and Denzel Washington and his supporting performers (Angela Bassett as Betty Shabazz, Al Freeman as Elijah Muhammad, and Albert Hall as Baines) are really charismatic, commanding actors.  But the subject matter and actors are let down by Spike Lee, who is constrained by two things.  One, the biopic format.  Two, his reverence and awe for Malcolm X.  As a result, the film is way too long, with the first interminable hour covering Malcolm Little's life as a petty criminal in Boston.  When he finally converts to the Nation of Islam, the film gets bogged down in Malcolm X's speeches.  And do not get me wrong, Washington brings a lot of pizzazz to the speeches, but they are shot in a rather boring way, with the repetitive panning crane shots drawing attention to themselves.  These are broken up by boring domestic scenes between Bassett and Washington, the former playing the "nagging wife" character.  The film really needed a tighter focus.

It misses the point, almost deliberately. By compressing the theological evolution that defined his final year into a hurried montage, the film prioritizes the sensational over the substantive. It seems more fascinated with the man he left behind than with the man he fought to become. This imbalance becomes even more glaring when compared to The Autobiography of Malcolm X which it's based on. Yes, the book is also a censored, edited, had major theology related chapters infamously auctioned off privately and withheld from publication. But even in its incomplete state, the autobiography understands something the film does not: that Malcolm X's story is fundamentally a spiritual conversion narrative. The book gives his post-Mecca transformation the weight and space it requires, allowing the reader to witness his ideological and religious evolution in real time. The film doesn't show that the NOI's un-Islamic anti-White theology lead to heightened racism, and only discovering mainstream orthodox Islam led to him having genuine hope for the first time. Spike Lee ultimately sacrifices the core of the story for a more conventional, easily-digestible piece of entertainment that appeals to a wider audience.

Do not be fooled by my 2.5 star rating, this film has enriched my life greatly. I didn’t like the film, BUT I am forever indebted to it for reconnecting me with the wonderful beautiful astounding film criticism of bell hooks. I finished the 3.5 hours of film feeling flat and irritated and seeing only praise on Letterboxd. And then I read two of hooks’ articles (Spike Lee’s Malcolm X and Male Heroes and Female Sex Objects: Sexism in Spike Lee's Malcolm X - both soo good) and also some bits of two of her books (Black looks: race and representation and Reel to Real: Race, Class and Sex at the Movies - also soo good). I literally cannot recommend them highly enough. Especially the two articles, they are so short and so true. She gave perfect voice to every irritation I had with the film. I genuinely think they should be mandatory reading alongside the film. But anyway, firstly, I thought this film was a warning against idolising individuals. My jaw was on the flooor reading other reviews, especially ones which acknowledge his misogyny but claim it adds realism or texture or something. If anything I feel like this stance legitimises the misogyny, because we acknowledge that he isn’t perfect so that we can continue to idolise him in peace ?? Idk, just generally hated the whole first hour and a half for that, and don't understand why this one random relationship took up so much screen time in a biopic of a man who did so many things. So needless, and even if it had fitted with the wider story I think there is a way to paint a portrait of a complicated man in a way which doesn’t use misogyny for viewer entertainment. ALSO the way in which Lee’s fictionalisation wrote important women like Ella Little-Collins out of history completely - unforgivable when there’s no apparent reason behind it and he literally claimed this film is meant to teach. And the way it hollywoodises Malcolm X and paints him as a lone wolf and completely ignores the reality of what community power looks like. Which brings me to my biggest complaint about depoliticisation - I feel like if you watched this film without knowing Malcolm X or anything about him, you would end up after 3.5 hours of film without any greater understanding of racial capitalism in the US. You hear some vague mentions of Black nationalism, you see a short bit of footage of police brutality but there's so much missing!!?! That said, I really liked this thing that bell hooks wrote: ‘like other bad movies with powerful subjects, it touches the hearts and minds of folks who bring their own meanings to it, connecting it with their own experience.’ And I definitely respect the project of introducing Malcolm X to way wider audiences, so there’s that. Anyway, everyone should read bell hooks!!

Trata-se, sem dúvida, de um filme incrível; todavia, o próprio fato de ser um dos mais relevantes filmes dedicados ao movimento dos direitos civis dos negros nos Estados Unidos revela, por si só, o modo peculiar, e não raro problemático, pelo qual a cultura de representação negra naquele país se organiza. Uma cultura que parece operar segundo uma lógica que bell hooks chamou de “plantação”, isto é, um regime simbólico no qual as imagens negras são simultaneamente administradas, moldadas e postas em circulação como mercadorias. Quando Spike Lee se propõe a transformar Malcolm X em uma marca, o lado originariamente subversivo de seu pensamento sofre um processo de diluição, tornando-se incapaz de ameaçar as forças de mercado que agora o absorvem e o comercializam. Tudo isso torna-se ainda mais evidente quando se observa que o filme, de maneira sistemática, elide ou marginaliza as críticas de Malcolm ao capitalismo, ao colonialismo e ao imperialismo , privilegiando, em contrapartida, aspectos de sua trajetória mais facilmente assimiláveis sob a forma de discurso religioso. Spike Lee suprime precisamente aquelas dimensões do pensamento malcolmiano que poderiam revelar-se mais perturbadoras para a sensibilidade dominante, convertendo-o, assim, em uma figura palatável ao homem branco, até porque, infelizmente, ainda é um filme hollywoodiano e eles precisam vender ingressos.

Nach etlichen Jahren habe ich mir endlich die Zeit genommen, den über drei Stunden langen Film Malcolm X zu schauen. Und ehrlich gesagt war ich lange unsicher, was mir der Film eigentlich erzählen will. Ich bin völlig unvorbereitet reingegangen und wusste weder im Detail, worum es geht, noch welche Richtung er einschlägt. Der Anfang plätschert für mich ziemlich vor sich hin, und erst nach etwa 25 Minuten wird es erzählerisch langsam interessant. Richtig klar wurde mir der Fokus aber erst nach rund einer Stunde, als sich der Film plötzlich wie ein Gangsterfilm anfühlt. Nochmals eine Stunde später schlägt er dann eine komplett andere Richtung ein und wird stark von radikal religiösen Themen geprägt. Mir ist absolut bewusst, dass Rassismus real ist und dass die Zeiten damals deutlich brutaler und ungerechter waren als heute, auch wenn der Blick auf Amerika 2025 oder 2026 leider zeigt, dass vieles noch immer nicht wirklich besser ist. Ich verstehe also, was der Film zeigen und vermitteln will. Trotzdem hatte ich persönlich kaum einen Zugang dazu. Ich habe keine Berührungspunkte mit radikalem Glauben und bin auch niemand, der rassistisch gegenüber anderen Menschen denkt. Genau deshalb hat mich dieses sehr belehrende Aufzeigen nicht immer abgeholt. Filmerisch ist der Film in Ordnung, leidet für mich aber deutlich unter dem sehr langsamen Tempo. Ich hatte mir insgesamt viel mehr erhofft. Als Dokudrama habe ich sowohl erzählerisch als auch filmisch schon deutlich stärkere Werke gesehen. Deshalb lande ich am Ende leider nur bei 5 von 10 Punkten, auch wenn mir bewusst ist, dass viele den Film ganz anders wahrnehmen und bewerten würden.

In less than 3 minutes I was reduced to tears as X's 1964 speech on the "American nightmare" played over footage of Rodney King being brutally beat by police only year before the release of this film. I felt a lot of the film that chronicled Malcom's earlier hustler lifestyle was unnecessarily long and overdramatised to appeal to a crossover audience (it did, people would not stop laughing). Lee did not need any acting role in this biopic at all, even if he may have not intended it, it seemed disrespectful to Malcom X's autobiography. I loved Denzel Washington performance in this film, its sadly ironic that he lost the Oscar to a white actor. However, I will say Washington's Malcom X lacked the rage, resistance Malcom X possessed, necessary for black militancy. The remainder of this film felt very cherry picked. Not once was Malcom X's condemnations of capitalism and colonialism included. The scariest part is I almost did not realise this until Bobby Seale and Nelson Mandela made a cameo and Angela Davis and the Black Panthers appeared in a montage for a split second. Unfortunately, yet again, Lee projects his Madonna-Whore complex unto his depiction of Malcom X and his relationship with women in this film (his educated progressive sister was simply just not included). I read bell hooks' critical essay about this film right after watching it, so I might be biased toward criticism here. But I think her points are important. She points out that key details of Malcolm's story have been changed, such as the role of his siblings in his conversion to Islam. She also points out that (Black) women in general are portrayed rather superficially, as "either virgins or whores, madonnas or prostitutes— and that’s Hollywood". And that Malcolm's criticisms of colonialism and capitalism are almost absent from the film – likely to make the film more palatable to white audiences. That said, it's still a powerful biopic. It's beautifully shot and powerfully acted. But it's also too Hollywood for its own sake.

skillsで鑑賞。リアペの課題が出ていたのでそれを添付 I watched the movie “Malcolm X”, and I was surprised and impressed by the way Malcolm’s identity changed over time. In his early life, his identity was deeply shaped by racism. However, in the end, he came to see himself as he truly was, without viewing himself through the lens of skin color. In this essay, I will discuss this transformation through three aspects that his name, institutional discrimination, and his experience in prison. Firstly, I was surprised that his name, Malcolm Little, is actually the named from white plantation owner. This was revealed when Malcolm was in prison and taught about black is not wrong via many things. His name, “Little” was not Malcolm’s family name, and it was taken from the name of his ancestor’s plantation owner. I think this was shocking because it shows how slavery took away people’s identity as they did not give the name from the very beginning, and it continues after many decades. Secondly, I was surprised that there is some invisible discrimination. When I hear “discrimination problems,” I always come up with some violent problems. Of course, Malcolm was a victim of physical violence due to discrimination, such as his father being killed by white people, but he was also affected by more subtle, mental discrimination. For example, he was a good student at school, despite being the only colored in his school, and he dreamed of becoming a lawyer. However, when he told his teacher, he was discouraged simply because he was Black. Another example, he always tried to straighten his curly hair to look more like a white person. He thought this made him better than other Black people. But later, he realized this way of thinking actually showed how much he had been influenced by white standards. This part was very interesting to me because there are some examples of invisible discrimination. Lastly, I was surprised that he finally found himself in “prison”. I had no expectation that an important figure like Malcolm X had once been a criminal, and it was also during his time that motivated to learn and proud of being black. He started to read some books and knew that words related to “black” had negative meanings while words related to “white” had positive ones, or that the first humans on Earth were in prison. These discoveries made him prouder as a black and triggered him to see himself without the perspective of white. In conclusion, Malcolm X’s story shows that identity can change through experience, knowledge, and reflection. Through his name, his experiences with discrimination, and his time in prison, he gradually freed himself from the influence of racism and came to understand his true self.

Theme/Subject: transformation Cinematic aspect: cinematography One expressive cinematography is the three different color pallets to paint the historical transformation Malcolm X had. Each color pallet reflects the three acts in the film. The first one (Act I) is shown to be warm and rich which represents his youth and his drug addiction since there was a crack epidemic ravaging  the black population. Then we move to Act II which contains one cool shade color that represents Malcolm X’s time in prison. When serving his time in prison Malcolm found his faith, Islam, and we get to Act III which is to be seen as more of the earthy type of color to represent him joining the National of Islam (NOI) and eventually Malcolm X left and went to Mecca he took the name of el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz. Each color shows different stages of his life. I think the opening montage really sets the mood for the film. It was an interesting way of incorporating history of violence against the black population mixed with the audio of Malcolm X along with the American flag slowly burning up and turning into the letter X. Right there and then you get a sense of what the movie will be about. When reading the textbook (pg 203-207) it was important that Lee wanted to shoot the Middle Eastern scenes in Africa rather than New Jersey. “It was a life-changing experience for Spike” (pg 204). Lee felt an instant connection where he saw the pyramid and the sphinx for the first time and thought those were his ancestors who built them. Scientists to this day don’t know how it was built. That scene in the film was the turning point for Malcolm X where he wanted to express more of an internationalist and anti-racism perspective. Heck “he [even] went to the high Islamic court again and again, until they finally agreed to allow for the first time a 35mm motion picture camera in the city of Mecca during Hajj” (pg 204). Even though the film was long (which I did not expect) I thought it was put together beautifully. I mean Denzel Washington was phenomenal. Denzel Washington est absolument monumental. Il ne se contente pas d'incarner Malcolm X : il accompagne toutes ses transformations, du petit délinquant charismatique au prédicateur radical, puis à l'homme qui remet progressivement en question ses propres certitudes. Sa présence porte une énorme partie du film. Le parcours de Malcolm est extrêmement bien construit. Le film ne présente pas un personnage figé, mais plusieurs versions successives d'un même homme. Ses convictions évoluent réellement à mesure qu'il découvre de nouvelles expériences, ce qui rend son parcours particulièrement intéressant. Le passage par La Mecque constitue notamment un véritable tournant idéologique plutôt qu'un simple événement biographique. La mise en scène de Spike Lee donne une vraie ampleur au récit. Le film alterne couleurs, noir et blanc, images d'archives et reconstitutions pour accompagner les différentes périodes de la vie de Malcolm. Le travail sur la photographie et celui sur les costumes donnent également une identité visuelle très forte au film. Ce qui fonctionne particulièrement bien, c'est que Spike Lee ne cherche pas à transformer Malcolm X en personnage héroïque. Il montre aussi ses contradictions, ses erreurs et notamment la radicalité de certaines de ses positions au sein de la Nation of Islam. Son évolution devient donc beaucoup plus intéressante : le film ne raconte pas simplement l'ascension d'un grand homme, mais montre comment ses expériences successives modifient sa manière de penser. C'est cette dimension intellectuelle qui donne au récit une véritable profondeur. Le film possède également une vraie force dans ses scènes publiques. Malcolm devient progressivement un orateur capable de captiver une foule entière, et Spike Lee sait parfaitement filmer cette transformation. Les discours ne sont pas uniquement là pour transmettre des informations : ils montrent la puissance de la parole et expliquent en partie pourquoi Malcolm est devenu une figure aussi influente. Denzel Washington donne à ces scènes une vraie intensité. J'apprécie aussi beaucoup le fait que le film conserve une dimension profondément personnelle. Derrière la figure politique, il y a l'enfant marqué par la violence raciste, le jeune homme perdu, le prisonnier, le mari et finalement l'homme qui cherche encore sa place et sa pensée jusqu'à la fin de sa vie. Cela évite que le film ne devienne uniquement une succession de discours historiques. Le film est trèèèèèèès long, 3h20, et cette ampleur peut donner une impression de lourdeur (énormément de discours finalement donc des parties inégales, plus intéressantes que d'autres donc pas facile de rester 100% focus). La première partie notamment prend beaucoup de temps pour installer les différentes étapes de la jeunesse de Malcolm. Certaines étapes de son évolution sont forcément condensées. Couvrir autant d'années et de transformations en un seul film implique parfois des transitions assez rapides entre différentes périodes de sa vie.

Scavenger Hunt #138 Film 1 of 30 Category: A film about activism. The Film *Malcolm X* is not simply a biography of an important man. It is the story of a person repeatedly destroying an old version of himself in order to become someone greater. Spike Lee refuses to present Malcolm as though he entered the world already prepared to become a leader. We see his anger, vanity, criminality, discipline, faith, pride, mistakes, and eventual willingness to reconsider beliefs that once defined him. The different names he carries represent those transformations. Malcolm Little is the child born into a family terrorized by racism. Detroit Red is the young man attempting to bury that pain beneath style, excitement, and crime. Malcolm X rejects the name inherited through slavery and replaces it with the unknown history stolen from him. El Hajj Malik El Shabazz emerges after Mecca with a larger understanding of humanity. Each name belongs to the same man, but none contains him completely. The early scenes are energetic and entertaining, but that energy hides enormous insecurity. Malcolm straightens his hair, changes the way he dresses, and performs a version of himself designed to survive and feel powerful. The conk becomes more than a hairstyle. It shows how racism can teach someone to reject features of his own body before he even realizes he is doing it. Prison becomes the place where physical confinement produces intellectual freedom. Malcolm begins reading, questioning language, and recognizing how history has been written by people with the power to define everyone else. Education does not merely give him information. It gives him a new understanding of himself. He discovers that controlling language means controlling the boundaries of what people believe is possible. The Nation of Islam gives Malcolm discipline, purpose, and a community, but the same organization that helps rebuild him eventually attempts to control him. His devotion to Elijah Muhammad is sincere, which makes the betrayal deeply personal. Malcolm realizes that replacing one form of dependence with another is not true liberation. He must be willing to question the person who taught him how to question everything else. His journey to Mecca becomes the film’s final great transformation. Malcolm does not abandon his understanding of racism in America, but he recognizes that his previous beliefs about race were incomplete. What makes him extraordinary is not that he was always correct. It is that he was willing to change publicly after building his identity around certainty. Many people would rather protect their pride than admit that experience has expanded their understanding. The Direction Spike Lee directs the film with the scale and confidence of an epic while keeping Malcolm’s personal evolution at its center. The opening immediately connects Malcolm’s life to the America that continued after his death. Images of the American flag burning into the shape of an X are combined with footage of Rodney King being beaten, making it clear that this is not a safely contained history lesson. The conditions Malcolm confronted did not disappear with him. Each period of Malcolm’s life has its own visual identity. The early sequences are colorful, playful, and alive with movement. Prison removes that freedom and replaces it with hard lines, shadows, and confined spaces. As Malcolm becomes a public figure, the compositions grow larger and more controlled, reflecting the authority he has developed. By the final section, that control begins collapsing under surveillance, threats, and betrayal. Lee never allows Malcolm’s speeches to become interruptions in the story. Speaking is the action. The film understands that Malcolm’s voice was his greatest instrument because he could transform private anger into a shared political consciousness. The crowds do not simply admire him. They recognize experiences that society repeatedly told them to endure quietly. The march to the hospital is one of the clearest demonstrations of his power. Malcolm controls the movement of an entire crowd with small gestures, revealing the discipline behind his leadership. The police see danger because they are witnessing a Black man exercise authority that does not depend upon their permission. The final movement carries an unavoidable sense of dread. Malcolm knows that death is approaching, but he continues speaking because fear can no longer determine the value of his work. The famous shot of him moving toward the ballroom makes him appear almost separated from the ground, as though history is carrying him toward a fate both he and the audience already understand. At more than three hours, the film is long, but that length mostly feels earned. Malcolm’s transformation would lose its meaning if any major stage were treated as a brief montage. Some supporting relationships are compressed because the film has so much history to contain, yet the overall scale allows Malcolm to feel like a full human being rather than a collection of famous speeches. The Acting Denzel Washington gives one of the greatest performances ever placed in a biographical film. He does not simply imitate Malcolm’s voice and physical mannerisms. He captures the intelligence, humor, anger, confidence, vulnerability, and constant mental movement beneath them. His performance changes with every stage of Malcolm’s life. Detroit Red moves with youthful arrogance, constantly trying to appear larger than he feels. The imprisoned Malcolm becomes quieter as his mind awakens. The public speaker controls rooms through rhythm and precision. The later Malcolm appears calmer but also more exposed because he is no longer protected by the certainty or organization that once surrounded him. Denzel is especially powerful during the speeches because he communicates why people followed Malcolm. The words are important, but so is the feeling that every sentence has been sharpened by personal experience. Malcolm does not speak about racism as an abstract political subject. He speaks as someone whose family, childhood, body, opportunities, and identity were all shaped by it. Angela Bassett brings strength and emotional clarity to Betty Shabazz. Betty is not merely the supportive wife waiting outside Malcolm’s public life. She understands the danger surrounding him and the cost his mission places on their family. Bassett shows the love between them while never pretending that loving someone with a historical purpose is easy. Delroy Lindo is also excellent as West Indian Archie, particularly when Malcolm encounters him years later. Archie’s decline becomes a vision of the future Malcolm escaped. Albert Hall gives Baines the calm authority necessary to make Malcolm’s religious transformation believable, while Al Freeman Jr. portrays Elijah Muhammad with enough warmth to make Malcolm’s eventual disillusionment feel genuinely painful. Conclusion *Malcolm X* succeeds because it refuses to freeze Malcolm into a simple symbol. He was not one thing for his entire life. He was a man capable of growth, contradiction, anger, tenderness, discipline, and change. The film respects him enough to show the journey rather than only celebrating the final image. His evolution does not weaken his legacy. It is the legacy. Malcolm teaches that identity does not have to remain confined by the name, history, or beliefs handed to us. A person can examine himself, reject what no longer serves the truth, and continue becoming someone new. The assassination is devastating because Malcolm dies at the moment his understanding is becoming widest. He has separated from the institution that once gave him power, broadened his view of humanity, and begun building something independently. The tragedy is not only that a great man was killed. It is that we will never know what his next transformation might have become. The final sequence expands Malcolm beyond one body. When people across generations declare themselves Malcolm X, they are not claiming to replace him. They are recognizing that his struggle for dignity, knowledge, and self definition belongs to everyone denied the right to define themselves. Spike Lee created something far greater than a standard biopic. He made a film about the courage required to confront the world and the even greater courage required to confront yourself. Malcolm’s power did not come from never changing. It came from refusing to stop.

Okay, Malcolm X . It’s a movie I’ve wanted to watch for a loooong time, but they added it to one of my streaming platforms yesterday, so I went for it without hesitation. And... I liked it quite a lot. I’m not going to go too deeply into Malcolm’s story because politics really isn’t my thing, and the film touches on a lot of subjects I don’t fully understand, whether because of my age, the cultural context, or simply because I haven't studied them enough. But there’s something about the historical context that really caught my attention. The United States, within a relatively short period, somehow managed to accumulate the assassinations of several politically or culturally significant figures (including a damn PRESIDENT) while certain government and law-enforcement agencies had an absolutely insane capacity for surveillance. When you look at things like MK-Ultra, or cases such as Harold Blauer and the experiments associated with Edgewood Arsenal, the extent of what was being done in the name of national security becomes pretty disturbing. Obviously, the government had lists of people considered threats or otherwise worth monitoring. Even John Lennon ended up on the authorities’ radar despite not being American, and Malcolm X was certainly being watched. His calls were monitored, his activities were followed, and agencies were gathering information on him under the usual collection of labels: suspicious, dangerous, security threat, or whatever happened to be convenient at the time. And yet, when Malcolm X was assassinated, apparently none of that surveillance gave them any idea that it was going to happen. That’s the part I find difficult not to question. The same government that had demonstrated an extraordinary capacity for surveillance, experimentation, and covert operations supposedly had no idea that one of the people it was closely monitoring was about to be assassinated. Maybe there’s a perfectly reasonable explanation. Maybe the information simply wasn’t there, or the agencies involved genuinely failed to connect the dots. I’m not claiming I have the answer, because I don’t. But when you put all of that together, it certainly makes you raise an eyebrow. Well... what a coincidence.

Religion is regarded by the common people as true, by the wise as false, and by rulers as useful. I don't know about the first two lines, but the last one still feels true even today. Religion can absolutely become a useful tool for rulers or people in power. In today's world, we call them politicians or sometimes even religious figures who claim to be God's servants. When you follow them blindly, you are praised as a devotee. But the moment you start questioning them, that's when the real problem begins. You don't get answers. Instead, hate is thrown your way. That only deepens your suspicions and slowly makes you realise what kind of world we live in --> where someone dictates what's right and what's wrong based on beliefs that have been planted into people's minds for years. I think Spike Lee tries to say something similar through Malcolm X . Religion or any faith, should guide a person into becoming a better version of themselves than they were yesterday. It should help you become a better human being who recognises everyone as equal. But when religion is used to build rage, spread hatred and discriminate against others based on race or colour, then it stops being a solution and becomes another problem added to an already existing one. Once hatred is passed down through generations, it isn't easy to erase. Even when the truth is right in front of you, accepting it means accepting that everything you've believed your whole life could have been a lie. That's not easy for anyone. When you can't question your beliefs and you can't accept the truth either, that's when blind faith takes over and blind faith only creates more hatred towards the people who dared to question it. When you don't question anything and simply follow blindly, consequences will always follow. By the time the truth reaches you, you won't even be ready to comprehend it. Brainwashing, whether done over generations or even over years, makes it much easier to hate, discriminate against and diminish another person than it is to love them. Love , Love is something every human being should possess. But people in power find it much easier to awaken hatred than compassion. People blindly follow them, become victims themselves and end up hurting both themselves and the people around them. That's exactly why Malcolm X's journey is so fascinating. He was once consumed by that blindness. He hated others based on race, colour and religion. He blindly followed those principles, preached them to others and built an entire movement around them. But the moment he started questioning everything and finally discovered the truth, his entire worldview shattered. He realised how wrong he had been and saw the damage his own words had caused to the people around him without ever knowing it. And look what happened when he finally chose to question that blind faith... What a pitiful world we still live in, driven by hatred in the name of race and religion. A faith built upon fear and hatred has brought this world far more wars than peace has ever known.

Once in a generation biopic? Once in a generation film? Once in a generation artistic achievement? I could hyperbolize about Malcolm X forever and I still would not be able to put into sufficient words just how monumental Spike Lee’s scrupulous account of this man is. No other visual rendition of a public figure can even approximate the effect of its testament to the significance of not just this individual life, but every individual life. It magnetizes with its ambition only to pull the viewer in further, further into its sweeping crevices that envelop the harrowing volatility of souls. Still so early in their illustrious careers, Denzel Washington and Spike Lee demonstrate a drive here that it’s difficult to say they ever had again (if anyone else has ever had it at all); their particular fortitude, courage, confidence, and determination as artists harmonize perfectly with their subject. From the first crackles of the smoldering Stars and Stripes, they reach for the limits of their capabilities and we are witnesses to an actor and his director refusing to deliver anything to the screen except undiluted inspiration. Just please watch this movie.

“Let it burn.” I've always considered Spike Lee's 'Malcolm X' my second-favorite of Lee's films, but revisiting it tonight, it certainly gives 'Do the Right Thing' a run for its money. It's a stunning balance Lee and Denzel Washington strike here between honoring the man and his place in American history and grounding the film as a character study through and through. The time spent on his time as "Red" in the streets of Harlem actually pays dividends in its sneaking patience, because you see the sweep of his life and why he was wayward and attracted to the Nation of Islam in the first place. As depicted here, it gave him a both a purpose and a purity of purpose, so much so that his purity was ultimately too much for others to accept. Regardless, the fire set to his childhood home became a burning rage within him, which was ultimately channeled for positive influence. Part of Lee's directorial brilliance, however, is in not putting a neat little bow around that positive influence and calling it a day, nor making the rage all-encompassing. His inclusion of historical and contemporaneous (to the film's release) news footage really works here, injecting righteous rage into well-hewn dramatic scenes which may or may not have anything to do with rage without feeling false to either tone. Of course, so much of the film's dynamism and clarity of purpose is due to the undeniably spectacular performance of Denzel Washington, in one of the many roles he was born to play. The resemblance is uncanny, and so too is the verve at every wavelength of the character. He commands the screen whether Malcolm is in command or not. This being Lee's best film from a visual perspective also develops that symbiotic relationship between actor and director. This is especially true in the sequence involving Malcolm's pilgrimage. That shot of him on the red prayer rug ensconced by those beautiful hanging lights is simply breathtaking. More than just mere visual beauty, it accomplishes everything the film sets out to do in framing this man and his expanding worldview at the center, but not the boundary of the broader civil rights movement and the evolution of humanist perspectives across the globe. Damn, maybe this has already become my favorite Spike Lee film and I don't even know it yet.
